intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene (607429) on chromosome 10p12.1.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: PDSS1 defect has been described in three patients from two families 6, 7 carrying three pathogenic variants in the PDSS1 gene, homozygous in one family and compound heterozygote in the other (Table 1).
checks.explanation: The paper describes homozygous and compound heterozygous PDSS1 variants causing CoQ10 deficiency. COQ10D2 is the standard OMIM name for this condition.

checks.claim: The PDSS1 gene is located on chromosome 10p12.1.
checks.evidence_quote: A genome-wide search for homozygosity in family 1 identified a region of chromosome 10 encompassing the gene prenyldiphosphate synthase, subunit 1 (PDSS1)
checks.explanation: The paper places PDSS1 on chromosome 10. The band 10p12.1 is standard nomenclature added by the draft.

paragraphs.text: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) biosynthesis. It reduces quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) activities. Reported clinical features include sensorineural hearing loss, optic atrophy, intellectual disability, muscle weakness, and cardiac valve involvement. One reported patient had a severe infantile-onset progressive multisystem disorder that was fatal in early childhood.

checks.claim: COQ10D2 is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Sequencing of PDSS1 identified a homozygous nucleotide substitution modifying a conserved amino acid of the protein (D308E).
checks.explanation: A homozygous mutation found by homozygosity mapping fits recessive inheritance, but the abstract never states autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: COQ10D2 is caused by a defect in coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis.
checks.evidence_quote: We have identified 2 novel inborn errors of CoQ10 biosynthesis in 2 distinct families.

checks.claim: COQ10D2 reduces quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) activities.
checks.evidence_quote: quinone-dependent OXPHOS activities were in the range of the lowest control values, while OXPHOS enzyme activities were normal. CoQ10 deficiency was confirmed by restoration of normal OXPHOS activities after addition of quinone.
checks.explanation: The paper says activities were in the range of the lowest control values, which is low-normal, and that adding quinone restored them. It does not plainly say they were reduced.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) reported 2 sisters born to consanguineous Egyptian parents. The older sister, a 16-year-old girl, was born after an uneventful pregnancy. At age 4 years she was found to have profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, which was treated with an externally powered prosthesis. She had severe language delay and mild intellectual disability. She also had progressive visual loss with red-green dyschromatopsia, optic atrophy, abnormal visual evoked potentials, and reduced thickness of the retinal nerve fiber layer. Other findings were diffuse mild muscle weakness and a mild postural tremor of the upper limbs. Her brain MRI was normal. Cardiac evaluation showed a dysplastic mitral valve with moderate insufficiency, tricuspid insufficiency, and a dilated left atrium. She did not have lactic acidosis, nephrotic syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, or macrocephaly. Her 6-year-old sister had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. At age 6 years she developed decreased visual acuity, and ophthalmologic examination showed optic atrophy, with bilateral pallor of the temporal sector of the optic nerve head, and divergent strabismus. She also had mild intellectual disability and muscle weakness with exercise intolerance. She had no cardiac valvulopathy, lactic acidosis, or nephrotic syndrome. Nardecchia et al. (2021) noted that in PDSS1 deficiency, unlike OPA1 and OPA3 defects, sensorineural deafness seemed to precede optic atrophy. They proposed that PDSS1 deficiency, a potentially treatable condition, be included in the differential diagnosis of optic atrophy with sensorineural deafness.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) reported a boy who presented at 5 months of age with failure to thrive, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, bilateral hearing impairment, pulmonary hypertension, livedo reticularis, and distal phalangeal erythema. Laboratory tests showed anemia, lactic acidosis, 3-methylglutaconic and tricarboxylic aciduria, and decreased CoQ10 levels in lymphocytes. He developed a progressive multisystem disorder that included severe developmental delay, pyramidal dysfunction, seizures, tremor, optic atrophy, nystagmus, severe visual and hearing impairment, cystic white matter changes, mild cerebral atrophy, and chronic heart failure. He died at 3 years of age.

paragraphs.text: Mollet et al. (2007) studied family 1 (see Mapping). Sequencing of the PDSS1 gene in this family identified a homozygous substitution that changed a conserved amino acid (D308E). When a yeast Delta-coq1 strain was transformed with a mutant yeast COQ1 corresponding to the D308E mutation, the strain grew poorly on respiratory medium. This finding indicated that the mutation causes the OXPHOS deficiency.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sisters from a consanguineous Egyptian family with COQ10D2, Nardecchia et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in the PDSS1 gene, resulting in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution. The variant affected a highly conserved residue (98.5% conservation across 184 eukaryotic sequences). It was absent from gnomAD and lay within a 12-Mb region of homozygosity. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. Of the unaffected sibs, a sister was homozygous wildtype and a brother was heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: In family 1 with CoQ10 deficiency, Mollet et al. (2007) identified a homozygous substitution in the PDSS1 gene resulting in an asp308-to-glu (D308E) change at a conserved residue. Quinone-dependent OXPHOS activities in this family were in the range of the lowest control values, and adding quinone restored them to normal. A yeast Delta-coq1 strain transformed with a mutant COQ1 corresponding to D308E grew poorly on respiratory medium.
